opus-5.5.text:
So this was a moment that really shifted my thinking. I'd been working on a calculation related to pulsars, specifically some of the electromagnetic structure around these rapidly rotating neutron stars, and at some point the problem reduced to evaluating an infinite sum. It's the kind of thing that shows up all the time in theoretical physics. You expand something in a series, you get a sum over modes, and then the question is whether you can actually get a closed form.

I'd spent a fair amount of time on it myself and hadn't cracked it. Partly as a test, partly out of curiosity, I gave it to o3 Pro. My expectations were honestly pretty low. I'd tried earlier models on technical problems and they'd often give you something that looked confident but fell apart when you checked it.

This time it went away, thought for a while, and came back with an answer, and it wasn't just an answer. It walked through the reasoning: how to rewrite the sum, which identities to use, how the pieces fit together. Then I checked it, both numerically and by going through the steps, and it was right.

That was a bit of a jolt. It wasn't a textbook exercise. It came out of an actual research problem, and the model handled it the way a strong collaborator would. It made me realize these tools had crossed a threshold. They weren't just retrieving things or pattern-matching surface features anymore. They could do a meaningful chunk of the technical work that eats up so much of a theorist's time.

It also changed how I think about my own workflow. If a model can reliably take on that kind of mathematical step, I can spend more of my energy on the parts I find most interesting: framing the right question, deciding what's physically meaningful, interpreting the results. You still have to verify everything carefully. That doesn't go away. But it made me take seriously the idea that AI could genuinely accelerate science, not in some distant future, but now.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I should say up front that I'm a theoretical physicist, and most of my work is in general relativity and black hole physics. The pulsar project was a bit of a side quest, but it involved exactly the kind of calculation that fills my days: you set up the physics, you reduce it to some horrible expression, and then you stare at a sum or an integral that you need in closed form.

In this case there was an infinite sum that had come out of the analysis, and I had a feeling it should collapse to something simple, because that's usually how these things go when the underlying physics is clean. But I couldn't see how. I'd tried the usual tricks, I'd fed it to Mathematica, and nothing was giving me a nice answer.

So, mostly out of curiosity, I gave it to o3 Pro. And I wasn't expecting much. My prior experience with language models on this kind of thing was that they would produce something that looked like a derivation, with all the right words, and then at some step they'd just assert a result that wasn't true. Very confident, very wrong, and you'd waste twenty minutes figuring out where it cheated.

What happened this time was different. It thought for a long time, and then it came back not with a closed form, but with an honest account: here's a transformation that gets you partway, here's why the obvious approach fails, and here's a representation that might be more tractable. And the partial result it gave was actually correct. I checked it. The reasoning held up step by step.

That was the thing that changed my view. It wasn't that it solved the problem, because it didn't fully. It was that it knew what it didn't know. It behaved like a strong graduate student rather than like a bluffing undergraduate. It gave me a genuinely useful intermediate step, it was transparent about where the difficulty was, and that intermediate step was enough for me to finish the calculation myself.

So the update for me was less "this thing can do my research" and more "this thing can be a real collaborator on the grinding technical parts." It can sit with a hard expression, try several approaches, tell you which ones are dead ends, and hand you something you can verify. For a theorist, that's a big deal. A lot of what slows us down isn't the ideas, it's the algebra between the ideas. If the model can reliably shoulder some of that, and be honest about its uncertainty while doing it, then it changes how fast you can explore.

I've become much more willing to throw the ugly parts of a calculation at it first, before I spend a day on them myself. I still check everything. But I check it the way I'd check a collaborator's work, not the way I'd check a suspect's alibi.

In research, you need to know whether a method applies, what assumptions it requires, and whether the result survives an independent check. Having o3 Pro attempt that sum put those questions front and center. It made me think about its abilities in terms of being a mathematical collaborator—something that can suggest a route worth exploring—while keeping responsibility for verifying the argument firmly with me.

sol-6.1.text:
It made me distinguish between being able to talk convincingly about a calculation and actually being able to carry it through. A sum is a very concrete test: you can check whether the reasoning works and whether the answer is right.

In research, though, the value isn’t always just the final answer. An attempted calculation can suggest a useful approach or expose an assumption you need to examine. So I began thinking of it more as a collaborator whose work I would check. The exciting possibility is that it can help move the calculation forward; the responsibility for verifying it still belongs to us.
